summary: Aims to focus discussion on problems of policy routing in the Internet and ways to solve them. It does not propose standards. Policy routing means choosing paths according to rules set by network owners, and not just by the shortest distance.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1102 discusses how network operators might choose routes according to administrative rules, rather than only path measures such as delay. The document proposes ideas for discussion and does not define an Internet standard.

questions: policy routing problems in the internet
how does a policy gateway check a route
what is an administrative region in rfc 1102
subtitle: A discussion of selecting Internet routes according to local administrative rules.

tldr.problem: Ordinary routing chooses paths using measures such as delay, but network operators may also need to restrict use according to customer class, service or cost policy.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes an abstract route made of administrative regions. The source selects that route, and policy gateways check it against local policy terms and choose concrete gateways.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1102 is a discussion of problems and possible solutions; it explicitly says that its proposals are not Internet standards.

sections.title: Why Routing Policies Matter
sections.content:
Routing protocols choose a path from available routes, often by minimizing a measure such as delay. Operators may also need to limit which classes of customers can use network resources, what service they receive or how costs are recovered.

The memo divides the Internet into Administrative Regions (ARs), each with its own administration and policies. A route across regions must satisfy the rules of each region it crosses.
sections.plainLanguage: Fastest-path routing does not express every network operator's rules. Different regions may set different conditions for carrying traffic.

sections.title: An Abstract Policy Route
sections.content:
A Policy Route (PR) is an ordered sequence of administrative regions. The source end point selects the sequence and attaches it to packets, rather than specifying every gateway in each region.

Each Policy Gateway checks whether the route is allowed and selects a concrete next gateway inside its region. This leaves operational gateway choices to the region while allowing the source to state the route's policy-level path.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender specifies which administrative regions a packet should cross. Gateways in those regions check the route and choose the next gateway.

sections.title: Policy Terms and Conditions
sections.content:
A gateway can compare an incoming route with local Policy Terms. A term can describe source and destination regions, the regions immediately before and after the current one, an optional user class and conditions.

Conditions might cover service type, time of day or accounting rules. The memo says conditions should be understood by end points in advance and should not depend on highly dynamic details such as queue length.
sections.plainLanguage: Each region defines terms that describe which routes it accepts. Those terms can include the users, neighboring regions and conditions that apply.

sections.title: Building and Selecting Routes
sections.content:
Route creation has two stages: synthesis finds sequences of compatible Policy Terms, and selection chooses one route that meets the user's conditions and preferences. The memo says synthesis may be automated, but selection can require human judgment when comparing costs or other conditions.

It proposes Policy Servers to store terms, synthesize possible routes, provide routes to hosts and help administrators set policy. Gateways may cache decisions as soft state that can be reconstructed after loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The system can find routes whose regional rules fit together. A user or administrator then chooses an acceptable route based on its conditions.

sections.title: Resource Use and Security
sections.content:
The memo discusses misuse of routes to consume network resources or charge for unauthorized use. It proposes sealing or signing routes at a Policy Server so gateways and other regions can check the source of the route.

The author describes detection and redress as possible ways to handle some misuse, and notes that additional study is needed. These are proposals in a discussion document, not finalized protocol requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal considers how regions might verify a route and account for its use. It leaves several details for further study.
